Newly emerged hatchlings of the Yellow-bellied toad (Bombina variegata) possess a minute body size, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0017 grams [Wwb = 0.0017 grams]. This remarkably low mass, typical of anuran species that produce large numbers of small eggs, is consistent with the early developmental stage at which the larvae enter the aquatic environment. The embryonic period is brief under favorable conditions, with eggs incubated at 19 °C [T = 19 °C] hatching after only 7 days [ab = 7 days], a short duration that reflects the warm, ephemeral ponds this species favors. At the onset of hatching, the jelly capsule surrounding each fertilized ovum dissolves, allowing the yolk-dependent tadpole to emerge. At this critical juncture, individuals measure approximately 1.5 centimeters  in snout–vent length, a size that marks the transition from the protective egg mass to an independent, free-swimming existence. The rapidity of this early development is an adaptation to breeding sites that may dry unpredictably, favoring accelerated yolk absorption and swift larval emergence.

During the subsequent aquatic tadpole stage, larvae progress through a series of Gosner stages characterized by steady somatic growth and the gradual development of limb buds. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant water temperature of 24.5 °C [T = 24.5 °C], the time elapsed since birth at metamorphosis is approximately 70 days . This relatively short larval duration is typical of bombinatorid frogs inhabiting temporary water bodies, where the risk of desiccation selects for rapid development. At the climax of metamorphosis, a profound body plan reorganization occurs, including tail resorption and the onset of pulmonary respiration, preparing the individual for terrestrial life. Following this transformation, the froglet emerges from the water weighing just a fraction of its future adult mass, carrying the energetic legacy of its larval feeding phase. Growth during this period is driven entirely by exogenous feeding on algae and detritus within the nursery pond, with no further reliance on yolk reserves.

Sexual maturation in Bombina variegata occurs after a protracted juvenile period. Measurements of wild-caught individuals indicate that the snout–vent length at puberty is 3.2 centimeters [Lp = 3.2 centimeters], a size threshold generally reached after approximately 547.5 days [tp = approximately 547.5 days] have elapsed since metamorphosis, based on data collected under natural thermal regimes averaging 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. This interval of about one and a half years post-metamorphosis reflects the time required for gonadal maturation and the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves for reproductive activity. During this sub-adult phase, individuals forage actively in terrestrial habitats, preying on small invertebrates to fuel both somatic maintenance and the development of reproductive tissues. The attainment of this size also corresponds to a shift in ecological role, as the growing juvenile transitions from a gape-limited predator to one capable of handling larger prey items.

Reproductive output in this species is modest compared to many tropical anurans but suited to its temperate-zone, ephemeral-pond breeding strategy. Field observations indicate that females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], consisting of up to 200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = up to 200 eggs per clutch]. This reproductive allocation is typical of bombinatorids, which invest relatively heavily in each clutch rather than spreading effort across multiple spawning events. The timing of reproduction is closely tied to spring rains, which fill temporary pools and provide the aquatic environment necessary for larval development. At the prevailing temperatures during the breeding season, approximately 14 °C [T = 14 °C], the onset of egg laying initiates a developmental schedule that capitalizes on the warm, shallow waters to maximize tadpole growth before pond desiccation. This single-clutch strategy also reduces the energetic burden on females, allowing them to allocate resources to subsequent survival and future breeding seasons.

Adult body size in Bombina variegata is among the smallest among European bombinatorids, with an ultimate snout–vent length reaching 5.6 centimeters [Li = 5.6 centimeters] and a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 12 grams [Wwi = 12 grams]. The maximum recorded longevity for this species, based on mark-recapture studies of wild populations in central Europe, is approximately 29 years [am = approximately 29 years], a lifespan that is remarkably high for a small anuran and underscores a slow-pace at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]d life history. This long adult duration under steady thermal conditions averaging 14 °C [T = 14 °C] allows for many breeding seasons, compensating for the modest annual reproductive output of a single clutch. The combination of a small asymptotic body size and a very long lifespan is unusual among frogs and suggests exceptionally low extrinsic mortality rates in the stable, predator-rich environments where this species persists. Senescence in these toads is characterized by a gradual decline in reproductive activity and body condition, with mortality ultimately resulting from physiological deterioration rather than predation.
